title: Inner humility (III.5–III.6)
hook: your name is called, every face turns, and out comes "oh, it was nothing"; Francis de Sales doesn't trust that answer
tomorrow: what if your anger is fair? why does Francis still shut the door?

segments.voice: Last time, patience: taking the trial as it comes, even in a line that won't move. The line was patience.

The gym is full. Someone at the microphone reads out a name, and it's yours. Every face turns. You walk up, take the certificate, someone says great job, and out it comes before you can stop it: oh, it was nothing. It sounds humble. It comes out almost by reflex. Francis de Sales, writing to Philothea, the reader of his book, doesn't quite trust that answer. What he thinks is going on under it is a little uncomfortable.
screen: `YOUR NAME, AND EVERY FACE TURNS.` → `OH, IT WAS NOTHING.` → `FRANCIS DOESN'T TRUST IT.`

segments.voice: Here's what he sees. First, look at the gift. Some people, Francis says, won't let themselves think about the good God has given them, for fear of pride. That's a mistake. Seeing a gift clearly, and seeing whose it is, leads to thanks and to love of the giver, not to vanity. Second, the words. We often call ourselves nothing, he says, misery itself, and we'd be stung if anyone took us at our word. Third, the motive. That kind of lowering, he says, can be a way of running off so that someone will chase us. Say it was nothing, and wait for someone to insist it was something. So the answer in the gym may be less humble than it sounds. Real humility, as he describes it, doesn't make a show or pile up humble words. It doesn't turn down a good task out of pretended modesty. Fourth, in the next chapter, he uses an old word, abjection, for our lowliness, and says the humble person comes to love it: being plain, or weak, or overlooked, or caught in a small clumsy moment. Not their faults, he's careful to say. Their smallness, carried gently, without fuss and without hiding it. Inner humility lets the truth be the truth, about the gift and about the smallness both. Sometimes the most honest answer is the shortest one.
screen: `LOOK AT THE GIFT.` · `CALLING YOURSELF NOTHING.` · `RUNNING SO SOMEONE CHASES.` · `SMALLNESS, CARRIED GENTLY.` · then, large: `TRUE HUMILITY.`

segments.voice: Bring back one real compliment you've been given, recent or old. Through the sit, let it be true without arguing with it, and then say, quietly, out loud: thank you. If you pray, thank God for the gift underneath it.
Inner humility. Humility in the heart, where only God sees it: honest about the gifts and about the smallness both.
Your line: true humility, the kind that can just say thank you. See you tomorrow.

notes: Introduction III.5 paraphrased: some refuse to consider God's gifts for fear of vainglory, which is a mistake, since considering them leads to love and thanks; we call ourselves nothing and misery but would be sorry to be taken at our word; we feign to fly so as to be pursued; true humility doesn't make a show or multiply humble words, and doesn't refuse good offices out of pretended humility. III.6: humility makes us love our own abjection (lowliness, not sin), with examples of being plain, weak, overlooked, or caught in small awkwardness. Confirm each, and the exact examples in III.6, against a standard edition.
'Abjection' is the word used in older English translations; confirm the English term and that 'not their faults' matches his distinction.
'Sometimes the most honest answer is the shortest one' and the carry's 'just say thank you' are the lesson's application, not Francis's words.
